claim: The zebrafish heart regenerates very efficiently and will regrow cardiac muscle without scarring.
source: The zebrafish heart regenerates very efficiently and will regrow cardiac muscle without scarring (Poss et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Poss et al., 2002

claim: Lineage tracing experiments revealed a model in which proliferation of preexisting cardiomyocytes replaces the myocardium that was lost during the injury.
source: Lineage tracing experiments revealed a model in which proliferation of preexisting cardiomyocytes replaces the myocardium that was lost during the injury (Jopling et al., 2010; Kikuchi et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jopling et al., 2010 and Kikuchi et al., 2010

claim: Cardiomyocyte proliferation in the uninjured adult zebrafish heart is very low.
source: While cardiomyocyte proliferation in the uninjured adult zebrafish heart is very low, 3 days after the injury (dpi) cardiomyocytes near the injury area (so-called border zone) start to reenter the cell cycle as observed by the induction PCNA expression, phosphorylated histone three and BrdU incorporation and proliferation peaks at 7 days post injury (dpi) (Jopling et al., 2010; Kikuchi et al., 2010; Chablais et al., 2011; González-Rosa et al., 2011; Schnabel et al., 2011; Wu et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: 3 days after the injury cardiomyocytes near the injury area start to reenter the cell cycle and proliferation peaks at 7 days post injury.
source: While cardiomyocyte proliferation in the uninjured adult zebrafish heart is very low, 3 days after the injury (dpi) cardiomyocytes near the injury area (so-called border zone) start to reenter the cell cycle as observed by the induction PCNA expression, phosphorylated histone three and BrdU incorporation and proliferation peaks at 7 days post injury (dpi) (Jopling et al., 2010; Kikuchi et al., 2010; Chablais et al., 2011; González-Rosa et al., 2011; Schnabel et al., 2011; Wu et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Border zone cardiomyocytes express cardiac transcription factors known for their role in embryonic heart development such as nkx2.5 and tbx20.
source: At the time when proliferation is observed, cardiomyocytes located in the border zone start to express cardiac transcription factors known for their role in embryonic heart development such as nkx2.5 and tbx20 and activate gata4 enhancer elements (Kikuchi et al., 2010; Lepilina et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kikuchi et al., 2010 and Lepilina et al., 2006

claim: Border zone cardiomyocytes show signs of dedifferentiation such as disorganization of sarcomere structures and the reexpression of embryonic myosins.
source: In addition, border zone cardiomyocytes show signs of dedifferentiation such as disorganization of sarcomere structures and the reexpression of embryonic myosins (Jopling et al., 2010; Wu et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jopling et al., 2010 and Wu et al., 2016

claim: 75% of the cardiomyocytes expressing high levels of nppa:mCitrine reentered the cell cycle at 7 dpi.
source: Histochemical analysis of cryo-injured adult hearts revealed that 75% (±7%, n = 3) of the cardiomyocytes expressing high levels of nppa:mCitrine reentered the cell cycle (Figure 1a).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from histochemical analysis and shown in Figure 1a

claim: In total 768 cells were sequenced in which 19257 genes were detected.
source: In total 768 cells where sequenced in which we detected 19257 genes.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental results from single-cell RNA sequencing

claim: An average of 10,443 reads per cell was detected in the single-cell RNA sequencing experiment.
source: We detected an average of 10,443 reads per cell and we introduced a cutoff at minimally 3500 reads per cell before further analysis, which resulted in the analysis of 352 cells.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental results from single-cell RNA sequencing

claim: A total of 12 cell clusters were identified in the single-cell RNA sequencing analysis.
source: A total of 12 cell clusters were identified, including a large group of cardiomyocytes (clusters 1,2,4,7 and 9), a smaller group of endothelial cells (clusters 5,6,8,10 and 12), and some fibroblasts (cluster 3) and immune cells (cluster 11) using the expression of marker genes for specific cell types (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by clustering analysis results and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: The cardiomyocytes fell into four main transcriptionally-defined clusters (1, 2, 4 and 7).
source: Based on the transcriptome clustering, the cardiomyocytes fell into four main transcriptionally-defined clusters (1, 2, 4 and 7), indicating that the injured heart contained subgroups of cardiomyocytes.
evidence: Supported by clustering analysis of single-cell transcriptome data

claim: The average mCitrine fluorescence intensity was highest in cluster 7 and lowest in cluster 2.
source: To address whether the border zone cardiomyocytes were enriched in one of the four cardiomyocyte clusters we compared the mCitrine fluorescence intensity (recorded during FACS sorting) of the cardiomyocyte and found that the average intensity was highest in cluster 7 and lowest in cluster 2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by FACS data analysis and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3

claim: Cells expressing nppa, vmhc and mustn1b were mostly in cluster 7.
source: In addition, we analysed the single-cell transcriptome data for the expression of nppa and compared this to the expression of vmhc and mustn1b, which mark border zone cardiomyocytes, and again found that cells expressing these genes were mostly in cluster 7 (Figure 1e and Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by single-cell transcriptome analysis and shown in Figure 1e and Figure 1—figure supplement 4

claim: Border zone cardiomyocytes (cluster 7) are transcriptionally distinct from remote cardiomyocytes (cluster 2).
source: Together, these results indicate two things: first, the border zone cardiomyocytes (grouped in cluster 7) can be identified as a separate group in the single-cell RNA-seq data. Secondly, these border zone cardiomyocytes are transcriptionally distinct from remote cardiomyocytes (grouped in cluster 2), while two intermediate cardiomyocyte clusters lie in between.
evidence: Inference based on clustering analysis and gene expression patterns

claim: Only 257 genes were differentially expressed between the embryonic and the cluster 7 (border zone) adult cardiomyocytes.
source: Importantly, the cluster seven cardiomyocytes identified in the adult data analysis had a transcriptome that was highly similar to embryonic cardiomyocytes, as shown by pairwise correlation of the differentially expressed genes between the cardiomyocyte clusters: only 257 genes (p-value<0.01), out of 23,786 total detected genes, were differentially expressed between the embryonic and the cluster 7 (border zone) adult cardiomyocytes (Figure 2d and Figure 2—source datas 1, 2, 3 and 4) suggesting a dedifferentiation of border zone cardiomyocytes to embryo--like cells.
evidence: Supported by differential gene expression analysis and shown in Figure 2d

claim: Over 1000 genes were differentially expressed between embryonic and cluster 2 (remote zone) adult cardiomyocytes.
source: In contrast, over 1000 genes (p-value<0.01) were differentially expressed between embryonic and cluster 2 (remote zone) adult cardiomyocytes.
evidence: Supported by differential gene expression analysis

claim: Cluster 7 cardiomyocytes were more closely related to embryonic than cluster 2 cardiomyocytes.
source: A heatmap with unbiased hierarchical clustering on the 500 most differentially expressed genes between the three clusters confirmed that cluster 7 cardiomyocytes were more closely related to embryonic than cluster 2 cardiomyocytes (Figure 2e).
evidence: Supported by hierarchical clustering analysis and shown in Figure 2e

claim: Genes encoding sarcomere proteins and cardiac-specific factors highly expressed in the embryo were re-expressed in cluster 7 (border zone) cardiomyocytes.
source: Corroborating the observation that border zone cardiomyocytes resemble embryonic cardiomyocytes we found that genes encoding sarcomere proteins and cardiac-specific factors highly expressed in the embryo were re-expressed in cluster 7 (border zone) cardiomyocytes (Figure 2f, g and h).
evidence: Supported by gene expression analysis and shown in Figure 2f, g and h

claim: There is a dedifferentiation axis from cells in cluster 2 (remote myocardium) to cells in cluster 7 (border zone myocardium).
source: Using this approach, we found large differences in transcriptome entropy, resulting in low (cluster 2), intermediate (clusters 1 and 4) and high (cluster 7) StemID scores (Figure 3a). This gradual increase suggests a dedifferentiation axis from cells in cluster 2 (remote myocardium) to cells in cluster 7 (border zone myocardium) and is in good agreement with our finding that the transcriptome of cluster 7 cardiomyocytes resembles an embryonic cardiomyocyte transcriptome (Figure 3b).
evidence: Supported by StemID analysis and shown in Figure 3a and 3b

claim: Clusters 4 and 7 are enriched for dedifferentiated and proliferative border zone cardiomyocytes while clusters 1 and 2 are enriched for differentiated remote cardiomyocytes.
source: Together, these results indicate that clusters 4 and 7 are enriched for dedifferentiated and proliferative border zone cardiomyocytes while clusters 1 and 2 are enriched for differentiated remote cardiomyocytes.
evidence: Inference based on StemID scores and gene expression patterns

claim: A 40% reduction in SDH activity was observed specifically in the border zone cardiomyocytes as compared to the remote cardiomyocytes.
source: To validate the functional consequences of the observed changes in mitochondrial gene expression, we measured succinate dehydrogenase (SDH) enzyme activity, located in the inner mitochondrial membrane that functions in both the citric acid cycle and electron transport chain. We observed a 40% reduction in SDH activity specifically in the border zone cardiomyocytes as compared to the remote cardiomyocytes (Figure 4a).
evidence: Supported by SDH enzyme activity measurements and shown in Figure 4a

claim: Transmission electron microscopy imaging revealed more immature mitochondria in border zone cardiomyocytes evidenced by their altered morphology and reduced cristae density.
source: In agreement with the reduced mitochondrial OXPHOS activity, transmission electron microscopy (TEM) imaging revealed more immature mitochondria in border zone cardiomyocytes evidenced by their altered morphology and reduced cristae density (Figure 4b), which is consistent with previous reports linking mitochondrial function with morphology (Giraud et al., 2002; Paumard et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by TEM imaging data and shown in Figure 4b, with citations to previous reports

claim: The GSEA revealed a strong and significant enrichment in the expression of glycolytic genes in cluster 7 cells compared to cluster 2 cells.
source: Since the pseudotime analysis suggested an upregulation of glycolytic gene expression in the border zone cluster (#7), we performed gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) for glycolysis genes. The GSEA revealed a strong and significant enrichment in the expression of glycolytic genes in cluster 7 cells compared to cluster 2 cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: Supported by GSEA analysis and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1c

claim: Induced expression of hexokinase (hk1), pyruvate kinase M1/M2a (pkma) and pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase (pdk2a) was confirmed in border zone cardiomyocytes by in situ hybridization.
source: By in situ hybridization we confirmed the induced expression in border zone cardiomyocytes of the rate-limiting enzymes hexokinase (hk1), pyruvate kinase M1/M2a (pkma) and pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase (pdk2a), which diverts pyruvate away from the TCA cycle (Figure 4c and Figure 1—figure supplement 4b).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data and shown in Figure 4c and Figure 1—figure supplement 4b

claim: Enhanced in vivo glucose uptake of border zone cardiomyocytes was observed.
source: Corroborating the suggested enhanced glycolysis, we observed induced expression of glucose importer genes (glut1a/slc2a1a and glut1b/slc2a1b) in cluster 7 cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1d) and enhanced in vivo glucose uptake of border zone cardiomyocytes (Figure 4d).
evidence: Supported by glucose uptake measurements and shown in Figure 4d

claim: Genes encoding lactate transporters and their proteins were upregulated in cluster seven and border zone cardiomyocytes.
source: Furthermore, genes encoding lactate transporters and their proteins were upregulated in cluster seven and border zone cardiomyocytes (Figure 4e and Figure 4—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: Supported by gene expression analysis and protein detection shown in Figure 4e and Figure 4—figure supplement 1d

claim: During regeneration border zone cardiomyocytes switch energy metabolism from mitochondrial OXPHOS to glycolysis and lactate fermentation.
source: Together, these data indicate that during regeneration border zone cardiomyocytes switch energy metabolism from mitochondrial OXPHOS to glycolysis and lactate fermentation.
evidence: Inference based on multiple lines of experimental evidence including gene expression, enzyme activity, and metabolite uptake

claim: Glycolysis gene expression is already induced at 3 dpi and thereby precedes expression of embryonic cardiac gene expression and cardiomyocyte proliferation, which peaks at 7 dpi.
source: The pseudo time line analysis suggested that glycolysis genes induction precedes the induction of embryonic cardiac gene expression. Indeed, ISH analysis showed that glycolysis gene expression is already induced at 3 dpi and thereby precedes expression of embryonic cardiac gene expression and cardiomyocyte proliferation, which peaks at 7 dpi (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by ISH analysis at different time points and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: Repeated injections of 2-DG in the adult zebrafish with a cryoinjured heart significantly impaired cardiomyocyte proliferation in the border zone.
source: We observed that repeated injections of 2-DG in the adult zebrafish with a cryoinjured heart significantly impaired cardiomyocyte proliferation in the border zone (Figure 5b,c), suggesting that glycolysis is necessary for cell cycle reentry.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from 2-DG treatment and shown in Figure 5b,c

claim: Glycolysis is necessary for cell cycle reentry of cardiomyocytes.
source: We observed that repeated injections of 2-DG in the adult zebrafish with a cryoinjured heart significantly impaired cardiomyocyte proliferation in the border zone (Figure 5b,c), suggesting that glycolysis is necessary for cell cycle reentry.
evidence: Inference based on the effect of glycolysis inhibition on cardiomyocyte proliferation

claim: When analysing cryo-injured hearts of Tg(phd3:GFP) fish 7 days post injury there was not a good correlation between pdh3:GFP reporter activity and the induction of ldha expression in border zone cardiomyocytes.
source: When analysing cryo-injured hearts of Tg(phd3:GFP) fish 7 days post injury we did not observe a good correlation between pdh3:GFP reporter activity and the induction of ldha expression in border zone cardiomyocytes suggesting that HIF signaling is not required for the observed induction of glycolysis gene expression in border zone cardiomyocytes (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by analysis of reporter line and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: HIF signaling is not required for the observed induction of glycolysis gene expression in border zone cardiomyocytes.
source: When analysing cryo-injured hearts of Tg(phd3:GFP) fish 7 days post injury we did not observe a good correlation between pdh3:GFP reporter activity and the induction of ldha expression in border zone cardiomyocytes suggesting that HIF signaling is not required for the observed induction of glycolysis gene expression in border zone cardiomyocytes (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Inference based on lack of correlation between HIF reporter and glycolysis gene expression

claim: A profound and consistent upregulation of glycolysis genes in the cortical myocardium was observed in Nrg1 overexpression hearts.
source: We observed a profound and consistent upregulation of glycolysis genes in the cortical myocardium coinciding with the reported cardiomyocyte dedifferentiation and proliferation in this layer (Figure 6a).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data in Nrg1 OE model and shown in Figure 6a

claim: Expression of ldha and hk1 was strongly induced in the ventricular wall of Nrg1 OE hearts.
source: Expression of ldha and hk1, encoding the rate limiting glycolytic enzyme hexokinase, was strongly induced in the ventricular wall of Nrg1 OE hearts, which correlates well with the observed induction of cardiomyocyte dedifferentiation and proliferation in this region (Gemberling et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data with citation to Gemberling et al., 2015

claim: The ErbB2 inhibitor AG1478 inhibited the induction of glycolytic gene expression in border zone cardiomyocytes.
source: qPCR confirmed the profound upregulation of glycolytic genes in border zone cardiomyocytes compared to their expression in cardiomyocytes from uninjured hearts (Figure 6b). Importantly the ErbB2 inhibitor AG1478 inhibited the induction of glycolytic gene expression in border zone cardiomyocytes (Figure 6b).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data with AG1478 treatment and shown in Figure 6b

claim: Glycolysis gene expression can be induced by Nrg1/ErbB2 signaling even in the absence of cardiac injury.
source: From these results, we conclude that glycolysis gene expression can be induced by Nrg1/ErbB2 signaling even in the absence of cardiac injury and that endogenous Nrg1/ErbB2 signaling is an important mediator of metabolic rewiring during zebrafish heart regeneration.
evidence: Inference based on Nrg1 overexpression experiments

claim: Endogenous Nrg1/ErbB2 signaling is an important mediator of metabolic rewiring during zebrafish heart regeneration.
source: From these results, we conclude that glycolysis gene expression can be induced by Nrg1/ErbB2 signaling even in the absence of cardiac injury and that endogenous Nrg1/ErbB2 signaling is an important mediator of metabolic rewiring during zebrafish heart regeneration.
evidence: Inference based on Nrg1 overexpression and ErbB2 inhibition experiments

claim: Critical glycolysis genes (e.g. Pfkp, Pdk3 and Pkm2) including glucose and lactate transporters (Slc16A3 and Slc2A1) were significantly upregulated in caErbB2 OE cardiomyocytes.
source: Indeed, we observed that critical glycolysis genes (e.g. Pfkp, Pdk3 and Pkm2) including glucose and lactate transporters (Slc16A3 and Slc2A1) were significantly upregulated in caErbB2 OE cardiomyocytes while genes transcribed from mitochondrial DNA were downregulated (Figure 6c).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data from caErbB2 OE mice and shown in Figure 6c

claim: Genes transcribed from mitochondrial DNA were downregulated in caErbB2 OE cardiomyocytes.
source: Indeed, we observed that critical glycolysis genes (e.g. Pfkp, Pdk3 and Pkm2) including glucose and lactate transporters (Slc16A3 and Slc2A1) were significantly upregulated in caErbB2 OE cardiomyocytes while genes transcribed from mitochondrial DNA were downregulated (Figure 6c).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data from caErbB2 OE mice and shown in Figure 6c

claim: An increased phosphorylation of PDH was observed in the inner myocardial layer of caErbB2 OE hearts.
source: Consistent with the increase in pdk3 expression, an increased phosphorylation of PDH was observed in the inner myocardial layer of caErbB2 OE hearts (Figure 6d).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data and shown in Figure 6d

claim: A stronger upregulation of glycolytic gene expression and decreased mitochondrial gene expression was observed in caErbB2 OE hearts with MI compared to wild type hearts with MI.
source: Even though glucose uptake and glycolytic enzyme activity in the ischemic area are increased by MI (Schelbert and Buxton, 1988) (Owen et al., 1969), we observed a stronger upregulation of glycolytic gene expression and decreased mitochondrial gene expression in caErbB2 OE hearts with MI compared to wild type hearts with MI (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data from MI experiments and shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1

claim: The stronger and consistent upregulation of glycolytic gene expression in caErbB2 OE hearts correlates with the reported enhanced cardiomyocyte proliferation and improved regeneration.
source: This stronger and consistent upregulation of glycolytic gene expression in caErbB2 OE hearts correlates with the reported enhanced cardiomyocyte proliferation and improved regeneration (D'Uva et al., 2015).
evidence: Inference based on correlation with previously reported findings, with citation to D'Uva et al., 2015

claim: Treating caErbB2 OE cardiomyocytes in vitro with the glycolysis inhibitors 2-DG or lonidamine strongly and significantly impaired cell cycle reentry.
source: Corroborating our model, we indeed observed that treating caErbB2 OE cardiomyocytes in vitro with the glycolysis inhibitors 2-DG or lonidamine strongly and significantly impaired cell cycle reentry (Figure 7b and c) and cytokinesis (Figure 7d and e).
evidence: Supported by in vitro experiments with glycolysis inhibitors and shown in Figure 7b and c

claim: Treating caErbB2 OE cardiomyocytes in vitro with the glycolysis inhibitors 2-DG or lonidamine strongly and significantly impaired cytokinesis.
source: Corroborating our model, we indeed observed that treating caErbB2 OE cardiomyocytes in vitro with the glycolysis inhibitors 2-DG or lonidamine strongly and significantly impaired cell cycle reentry (Figure 7b and c) and cytokinesis (Figure 7d and e).
evidence: Supported by in vitro experiments with glycolysis inhibitors and shown in Figure 7d and e

claim: In murine cardiomyocytes, ErbB2 signaling drives a metabolic switch towards glycolysis, which is required for their cell cycle reentry.
source: Together these results indicate that in murine cardiomyocytes, ErbB2 signaling drives a metabolic switch towards glycolysis, which is required for their cell cycle reentry.
evidence: Inference based on multiple experiments showing ErbB2-induced glycolysis and requirement for proliferation

claim: The metabolic switch in cardiomyocytes is beneficial for heart regeneration.
source: These results suggest that this metabolic switch in cardiomyocytes is beneficial for heart regeneration.
evidence: Speculation based on experimental results

claim: The mammalian adult heart has very little regenerative capacity.
source: The mammalian adult heart has very little regenerative capacity.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge

claim: The myocardium lost after an injury is replaced by scar tissue, which does not contribute to cardiac contraction resulting in reduced pumping efficiency and ultimately heart failure.
source: The myocardium lost after an injury is replaced by scar tissue, which does not contribute to cardiac contraction resulting in reduced pumping efficiency and ultimately heart failure.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge

claim: There is no evidence of a stem cell population in the mammalian heart.
source: Although a low level of cardiomyocyte turnover has been observed, there is no evidence of a stem cell population in the mammalian heart (Kretzschmar et al., 2018; van Berlo et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kretzschmar et al., 2018 and van Berlo et al., 2014

claim: A rare population of endogenous cardiomyocytes retains the capacity to proliferate to maintain cardiac homeostasis.
source: Instead, a rare population of endogenous cardiomyocytes retains the capacity to proliferate to maintain cardiac homeostasis (Bergmann et al., 2009; Bergmann et al., 2015; Kimura et al., 2015; Senyo et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: The neonatal mouse and potentially human heart still have the capacity to regenerate after injury.
source: Contrary to the adult heart, the neonatal mouse and potentially human heart still have the capacity to regenerate after injury (Haubner et al., 2016; Porrello et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Haubner et al., 2016 and Porrello et al., 2011

claim: The regenerative capacity of the neonatal heart involves proliferation of pre-existing cardiomyocytes and is lost soon after birth most likely due to a sharp decrease in cardiomyocyte proliferation.
source: This regenerative capacity of the neonatal heart involves proliferation of pre-existing cardiomyocytes and is lost soon after birth most likely due to a sharp decrease in cardiomyocyte proliferation (Porrello et al., 2011; Soonpaa et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to Porrello et al., 2011 and Soonpaa et al., 1996

claim: Inhibiting Hippo signaling or activating the Nrg1/ErbB2 signaling pathway in the adult mammalian heart enhances proliferation of cardiomyocytes.
source: Recent efforts to enhance proliferation of cardiomyocytes by either inhibiting Hippo signaling or activating the Nrg1/ErbB2 signaling pathway in the adult mammalian heart have been successful and show the potential of existing cardiomyocytes to reenter the cell cycle. (Bersell et al., 2009; D'Uva et al., 2015; Heallen et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bersell et al., 2009, D'Uva et al., 2015, and Heallen et al., 2011

claim: Increased mitochondrial OXPHOS activity promotes cardiomyocyte maturation and reduces the proliferative capacity of cardiomyocytes.
source: Increased mitochondrial OXPHOS activity promotes cardiomyocyte maturation and reduces the proliferative capacity of cardiomyocytes (Mills et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mills et al., 2017

claim: The metabolism in cardiomyocytes changes from predominantly glycolysis to mitochondrial OXPHOS in the first week after birth in mice.
source: This correlates well with the loss of regenerative capacity of the murine heart in the first week after birth at which time the metabolism in cardiomyocytes changes from predominantly glycolysis to mitochondrial OXPHOS (Lopaschuk et al., 1992; Menendez-Montes et al., 2016; Porrello et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lopaschuk et al., 1992, Menendez-Montes et al., 2016, and Porrello et al., 2011

claim: Reactive oxygen species (ROS) generated by mitochondrial OXPHOS induce DNA damage causing cardiomyocyte cell-cycle arrest.
source: Reactive oxygen species (ROS) generated by mitochondrial OXPHOS induce DNA damage causing cardiomyocyte cell-cycle arrest (Nakada et al., 2017; Puente et al., 2014; Tao et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Nakada et al., 2017, Puente et al., 2014, and Tao et al., 2016

claim: A similar metabolic shift from mitochondrial OXPHOS to glycolysis and lactate fermentation occurs in proliferating tumor cells, first described by Otto Warburg.
source: Interestingly, a similar metabolic shift from mitochondrial OXPHOS to glycolysis and lactate fermentation occurs in proliferating tumor cells, and was first described by Otto Warburg (Warburg et al., 1927).
evidence: Supported by citation to Warburg et al., 1927

claim: Glycolysis and the connected pentose-phosphate pathway provides essential metabolites that are needed to create sufficient biomass to sustain proliferation of tumor cells.
source: While glycolysis generates much less ATP compared to fatty acid oxidation, it is thought that glycolysis and the connected pentose-phosphate pathway provides essential metabolites that are needed to create sufficient biomass to sustain proliferation of the tumor cells (Vander Heiden et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vander Heiden et al., 2009

claim: Progenitor cells in the developing embryo as well as induced pluripotent stem cells depend on glycolysis to maintain proliferation and their potency.
source: Furthermore, progenitor cells in the developing embryo as well as induced pluripotent stem cells depend on glycolysis to maintain proliferation and their potency (Folmes et al., 2011; Gu et al., 2016; Mathieu and Ruohola-Baker, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Folmes et al., 2011, Gu et al., 2016, and Mathieu and Ruohola-Baker, 2017

claim: Glycolytic enzymes such as PKM2 and PFKFB4 can directly interact with cell cycle regulators to promote proliferation.
source: In addition, glycolytic enzymes such as PKM2 and PFKFB4 can also directly interact with cell cycle regulators to promote proliferation (Yang et al., 2011; Dasgupta et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Yang et al., 2011 and Dasgupta et al., 2018

claim: Activation of Nrg1/ErbB2 signaling in either zebrafish or mouse hearts induces cardiomyocyte dedifferentiation and proliferation.
source: Activation of Nrg1/ErbB2 signaling in either zebrafish or mouse hearts induces cardiomyocyte dedifferentiation and proliferation (D'Uva et al., 2015; Gemberling et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to D'Uva et al., 2015 and Gemberling et al., 2015

claim: Nrg1/ErbB2 signaling induces profound metabolic reprogramming in cardiomyocytes and this is required for efficient cardiomyocyte proliferation.
source: Our results build upon these observations and indicate that Nrg1/ErbB2 signaling induces profound metabolic reprogramming in cardiomyocytes and that this is required for efficient cardiomyocyte proliferation.
evidence: Inference based on experimental results from this study

claim: Activation of Yap signaling in the murine heart promotes cardiomyocyte proliferation, which involves a partial reprogramming and dedifferentiation of adult cardiomyocytes towards a neonatal fate.
source: Activation of Yap signaling in the murine heart promotes cardiomyocyte proliferation, which involves a partial reprogramming and dedifferentiation of adult cardiomyocytes towards a neonatal fate (Monroe et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Monroe et al., 2019

claim: Single-cell RNA-seq analysis of connective tissue cells during limb blastema formation revealed that their transcriptome is highly similar to embryonic limb precursor cells.
source: Interestingly, single-cell RNA-seq analysis of connective tissue cells during limb blastema formation revealed that their transcriptome is highly similar to embryonic limb precursor cells (Gerber et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gerber et al., 2018

claim: Adult tissues that lack a clear stem cell use an alternative strategy to regenerate the missing tissue by reprogramming differentiated cells into embryo-like cells.
source: Together with our results that a similar reprogramming takes place during injury induced heart regeneration in zebrafish it suggests a common theme in which adult tissues that lack a clear stem cell use an alternative strategy to regenerate the missing tissue by reprogramming differentiated cells into embryo-like cells.
evidence: Inference based on comparison of findings from this study with other regeneration studies

claim: Yap signaling is not required for cardiomyocyte proliferation during zebrafish heart regeneration.
source: This might involve different mechanisms since Yap signaling is not required for cardiomyocyte proliferation during zebrafish heart regeneration (Flinn et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Flinn et al., 2019

claim: The presence of embryo-like cardiomyocytes in the border zone after injury can explain the observed switch from trabecular cardiomyocytes into cortical cardiomyocytes during zebrafish heart regeneration.
source: The presence of embryo-like cardiomyocytes in the border zone after injury can explain the observed switch from trabecular cardiomyocytes into cortical cardiomyocytes during zebrafish heart regeneration, since embryonic cardiomyocytes give rise to both trabecular and cortical cardiomyocytes (Sánchez-Iranzo et al., 2018; Staudt et al., 2014).
evidence: Inference based on findings from this study and citations to Sánchez-Iranzo et al., 2018 and Staudt et al., 2014
